subject: Cognitive Science
title: Predictive Processing
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Predictive Processing.

hook.text: Your brain doesn't wait for input. It generates a prediction of what's coming and checks it against reality.

buildup.text: Karl Friston's framework says the brain is a prediction machine, constantly running a model of the world.

discovery.text: When predictions match input, nothing happens. When they don't, a prediction error signal fires—and you notice.

twist.text: This means perception is mostly hallucination constrained by data. You see your expectations, corrected by senses.

climax.text: Anxiety may be a prediction error disorder—the brain constantly predicting threats that never arrive.

punchline.text: You perceive what you expect—and only notice when you're wrong.

quiz.question: What fires when perception doesn't match prediction?

details.summary: Predictive processing theory proposes that the brain constantly generates predictions about incoming sensory data and only processes the prediction errors, the surprises. Perception is dominated by what the brain expects, not what the senses report. Surprise is the signal that matters.
details.whyItMatters: Predictive processing is becoming the leading theory of how brains work. It unifies perception, action, attention, and even mental illness under one framework.
takeaways: The brain predicts sensory input before it arrives
Only prediction errors are processed in detail
This framework unifies perception, action, and attention

faq.question: How does predictive processing explain illusions?
faq.answer: Illusions occur when the brain's predictions override actual sensory input. If your model strongly predicts a certain shape, color, or motion, you perceive the prediction rather than the raw data.

faq.question: What happens when predictions are wrong?
faq.answer: Prediction errors generate surprise signals that propagate upward through the brain. Strong errors trigger attention and learning: the brain updates its model to make better predictions next time. This is how the brain learns from experience and adapts to changing environments.
